claim: D. melanogaster and D. virilis are separated by 1.4 substitutions per neutral site.
source: Here, we assayed the binding of five essential TFs over multiple stages of embryogenesis in two distant Drosophila species (with 1.4 substitutions per neutral site)
evidence: The manuscript directly states the evolutionary distance between the two species in terms of neutral substitutions.

claim: The five transcription factors examined (Twi, Mef2, Tin, Bap, Bin) are major drivers of mesoderm subdivision into different muscle primordia.
source: The five factors examined, Twi, Mef2, Tinman (Tin), Bagpipe (Bap) and Biniou (Bin), are the major drivers of the subdivision of the mesoderm into different muscle primordia and form part of a highly interconnected gene regulatory network (Figure 1a) (Bonn and Furlong, 2008; Jakobsen et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2009; Sandmann et al., 2007, 2006; Zinzen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies and reference to Figure 1a showing the regulatory network.

claim: Approximately 2800 orthologous cis-regulatory elements were identified between D. melanogaster and D. virilis.
source: Using these signatures of TF occupancy, we identified a conservative set of ~2800 orthologous cis-regulatory elements and examined their combinatorial and dynamic occupancy across five embryonic time-points.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of orthologous elements identified in the study.

claim: Conserved TF binding was observed despite reduced sequence dependency when TFs are combinatorially bound with other factors.
source: In addition, we also observed the converse, conserved TF binding associated with reduced sequence dependency, when the TF is combinatorially bound with other factors.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from their cross-species analysis.

claim: The interferon beta enhancer is the best studied, and perhaps only true enhanceosome.
source: The best studied, and perhaps only true enhancesome, is the interferon beta enhancer, a 57 bp core element with a very strict arrangement of TFBS (Panne et al., 2007; Thanos and Maniatis, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on the interferon beta enhancer.

claim: The TF collective model predicts that enhancers should tolerate some evolutionary changes in TFBS content while having little or no effect on TF occupancy across species.
source: One prediction from this model is that such enhancers should tolerate some evolutionary changes in TFBS content, while having little or no effect on TF occupancy across species, as recently observed for the distal-less enhancer occupied by a Hox TF collective (Uhl et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this prediction and provides a citation to supporting evidence.

claim: Approximately 60% of sites bound by Twist have conserved occupancy between D. melanogaster and D. pseudoobscura.
source: For example,~60% of sites bound by the developmental master regulator Twist (Twi) have conserved occupancy between Drosophila melanogaster and pseudoobscura (He et al., 2011), an evolutionary distance comparable to that between human and chicken (estimated 1.1 substitutions per neutral site (Stark et al., 2007)).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to He et al., 2011 and comparison to evolutionary distance.

claim: Only 14% of CEBPA binding is conserved between human and mouse in adult liver.
source: For instance, in the adult liver, only 14% of CEBPA binding are conserved between human and mouse (Schmidt et al., 2010), species separated by ~60 million years (0.5 substitutions per neutral sites [Stark et al., 2007]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2010.

claim: The rate of evolution or divergence in TF binding is similar between vertebrates and flies when analyzed using a unifying statistical framework.
source: When the datasets were re-analyzed using a unifying statistical framework, which alleviates differences in analytical methods (Carvunis et al., 2015), the rate of evolution or divergence in TF binding are similar between vertebrates and flies, suggesting that transcriptional networks evolve at a common rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Carvunis et al., 2015 and their re-analysis.

claim: The molecular distance between D. melanogaster and D. virilis is approximately 3 times that between human and mouse.
source: These two species are highly diverged (neutral substitutions per base of 1.4) with an estimated molecular distance ~3 times that between human and mouse (Stark et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stark et al., 2007.

claim: Species-specific antibodies were generated for D. virilis proteins Tin, Twi, Bin, and Bap.
source: To circumvent potential technical inconsistencies due to reduced antibody affinity across species, we generated new antibodies for four TFs directed against the full-length D. virilis proteins: Tin, Twi, Bin and Bap.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the generation of new antibodies for the study.

claim: The D. melanogaster Mef2 antibody performed equally well for both D. virilis and D. melanogaster embryos.
source: For Mef2, the D. melanogaster antibody performed equally well using D. virilis or D. melanogaster embryos for both ChIP-qPCR (Materials and methods) and immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references supporting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All five antibodies gave highly specific and dynamic patterns of expression in D. virilis embryos.
source: Importantly, all five antibodies gave the expected, highly specific and dynamic patterns of expression in D. virilis embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), demonstrating the specificity of the antibodies and the conservation in the spatio-temporal expression patterns of these TFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing immunostaining patterns.

claim: ChIP-seq was performed in D. virilis embryos across five time windows of embryogenesis.
source: ChIP-seq was performed in D. virilis embryos across five time windows of embryogenesis, equivalent to those we previously used to analyze these transcription factors occupancy in D. melanogaster (Zinzen et al., 2009) (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design with reference to Figure 1b,c.

claim: Two independent biological replicates were generated for all TFs across all time-points.
source: For all TFs across all corresponding time-points, two independent biological replicates were generated, using two independent sera when possible (Twi, Mef2), leading to a total of 28 D. virilis ChIP-seq datasets and 10 stage-matched genomic input controls (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the number of replicates and datasets generated.

claim: Replicates were highly reproducible with median Pearson correlation Rho = 0.83 for raw reads.
source: Replicates were highly reproducible for both raw reads (median Pearson correlation Rho = 0.83) and significant TF peaks (median Pearson correlation Rho = 0.82).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific correlation values demonstrating reproducibility.

claim: De novo motif discovery systematically identified the expected motifs enriched under TF peak summits.
source: In addition, de novo motif discovery systematically identified the expected motifs enriched under the TF peak summits, attesting to the quality of the D. virilis ChIP-data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing motif logos.

claim: The number of peaks was generally higher for each TF in D. virilis ChIP-seq compared to D. melanogaster ChIP-chip data.
source: The number of peaks was generally higher for each TF in the D. virilis ChIP-seq compared to their corresponding D. melanogaster ChIP-chip data (Zinzen et al., 2009) (Figure 1d, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with reference to Figure 1d and supplementary data.

claim: The larger number of peaks in D. virilis potentially reflects the larger size of the D. virilis non-coding genome or higher sensitivity of ChIP-seq versus ChIP-chip.
source: The number of peaks was generally higher for each TF in the D. virilis ChIP-seq compared to their corresponding D. melanogaster ChIP-chip data (Zinzen et al., 2009) (Figure 1d, Supplementary file 1), potentially reflecting the larger size of the D. virilis non-coding genome (which we estimate is approximately 50% larger) or the higher sensitivity of ChIP-seq versus ChIP-chip.
evidence: The manuscript provides two potential explanations for the observed difference in peak numbers.

claim: 89% of D. virilis bound peaks were successfully translated to D. melanogaster coordinates using pslMap.
source: The peaks identified in D. virilis were then translated onto D. melanogaster coordinates using pslMap (Zhu et al., 2007), resulting in 89% of bound peaks translated (Materials and methods, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage of peaks successfully translated.

claim: Early in embryogenesis, Mef2 binds to a small number of regions and the binding is highly diverged amongst species.
source: Early in embryogenesis Mef2 binds to a small number of regions and the binding is highly diverged amongst species.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation about Mef2 binding patterns.

claim: By mid- and late-embryogenesis, both the number and conservation in Mef2 binding is substantially higher.
source: In contrast, by mid- and late- embryogenesis both the number and conservation in Mef2 binding is substantially higher (Figure 1d,e; compare TP1, 2 to TP3-5), matching the essential role of Mef2 in muscle differentiation at these later embryonic stages.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with reference to Figure 1d,e showing the data.

claim: The occupancy of Twi and Tin are highly conserved over all time-windows examined, with on average ~50% conservation in binding.
source: In contrast, the occupancy of Twi and Tin are highly conserved over all time-windows examined, with on average ~50% conservation in binding.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the conservation percentage for Twi and Tin.

claim: Only ~19% of Bap's and 26% of Bin's occupancy is conserved between D. melanogaster and D. virilis.
source: In contrast, only ~19% of Bap's and 26% of Bin's occupancy is conserved (Figure 1e, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the conservation percentages with reference to Figure 1e.

claim: Both Bap and Bin are essential for the specification of the visceral muscle primordial.
source: yet both TFs are essential for the specification of the visceral muscle primordial, and Bin for its subsequent differentiation (Jakobsen et al., 2007; Zaffran et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss-of-function bap or bin mutant embryos develop no gut muscle and are embryonic lethal.
source: loss-of-function bap or bin mutant embryos develop no gut muscle and are therefore embryonic lethal (Azpiazu and Frasch, 1993; Zaffran et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FoxF TFs (orthologs of Bin) are essential for gut muscle development in both mice and Xenopus.
source: It is interesting to note that the orthologs of Bin, FoxF TFs, are also essential for gut muscle development in both mice (Ormestad et al., 2006) and Xenopus (Tseng et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in mice and Xenopus.

claim: 95% of D. melanogaster ChIP-CRMs function as developmental enhancers in vivo in stable transgenic embryos.
source: Importantly, 95% of the elements tested (with an average size of 271 bases), function as developmental enhancers in vivo in stable transgenic embryos, as seen from a number of studies (Cannavò et al., 2016; Ciglar et al., 2014; Junion et al., 2012; Zinzen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies that tested these elements.

claim: 14,385 non-overlapping CRMs with an average size of 273 bases were defined in D. virilis.
source: Here, we grouped the set of 33,285 significant D. virilis ChIP peaks, spanning all TFs and all time-points, into a high-confidence set of 14,385 non-overlapping CRMs, with an average size of 273 bases (Materials and methods, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and size of CRMs defined.

claim: Fewer than half of D. melanogaster CRMs (44%; 3497/8008) overlap a D. virilis CRM.
source: Fewer than half of D. melanogaster CRMs (44%; 3497/8008, Figure 1g), overlap a D. virilis CRM (median overlap of 170 bp, corresponding to 62% median CRM length)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage and number with reference to Figure 1g.

claim: 2846 CRMs are in orthologous regions in a one-to-one relationship between D. melanogaster and D. virilis.
source: 2846 CRMs are in the orthologous region in a one-to-one relationship (Figure 1f), while an additional 651 D. melanogaster CRMs overlap two or more adjacent D. virilis CRMs.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of one-to-one orthologous CRMs.

claim: Less than half of human CRMs were found in an orthologous position in another vertebrate species.
source: Interestingly, this overlap is very similar to that observed in humans, where less than half of CRMs were found in an orthologous position in another vertebrate species (Ballester et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ballester et al., 2014.

claim: Only 14% (404/2846) of orthologous CRMs are bound by a single TF at a single time-point in both species.
source: Of the 2846 orthologous CRMs, only 14% (404/2846 elements) are bound by a single TF at a single time-point in both species, with the vast majority (86%, 2442 elements) being bound by multiple TFs and/or at multiple developmental stages in one or the other species.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage and number of single-TF bound CRMs.

claim: The 2442 cross-species multi-ChIP peak CRM pairs were distributed into three binding conservation categories: strong (J >= 0.5; 812 CRMs), intermediate (0 < J < 0.5; 1130 CRMs), and no binding conservation (J = 0; 500 CRMs).
source: Based on this systematic indexing, the 2442 cross-species multi-ChIP peak CRM pairs were distributed into three binding conservation categories; those with strong (J >= 0.5; 812 CRMs, Supplementary file 4), intermediate (0 < J < 0.5; 1130 CRMs, Supplementary file 5) and no binding conservation (J = 0; 500 CRMs, Supplementary file 6) (Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the categorization with specific numbers and Jaccard index thresholds.

claim: Enhancers with conserved TF binding have a higher number of total TF binding events in D. melanogaster compared to ones with no conservation.
source: Enhancers with conserved TF binding (both strong and intermediate levels) have a higher number of total TF binding events in D. melanogaster, i.e. more combinatorial occupancy compared to ones with no conservation (Figure 2b, Chi-square test p-value=5e−04 for each of the three pairwise comparisons), as expected (Paris et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with statistical support and reference to Figure 2b.

claim: 494 (20.3%) CRMs in orthologous pairs have been experimentally tested in D. melanogaster and shown to function as developmental enhancers in vivo.
source: Overlapping our inter-species CRMs bound by mesoderm/muscle TFs with these enhancers indicates that 494 (20.3%; 494/2442) CRMs in an orthologous pair have been experimentally tested in D. melanogaster and shown to function as developmental enhancers in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and percentage of tested enhancers.

claim: CRMs with strong and intermediate conservation in their occupancy have significantly higher overlap with characterized mesodermal and muscle enhancers compared to CRMs with non-conserved binding.
source: Importantly, CRMs with strong and intermediate conservation in their occupancy (based on their Jaccard similarity coefficient) have significantly higher overlap with characterized mesodermal and muscle enhancers compared to CRMs with non conserved binding (Figure 2d, two-sided proportions test p-value=5.3e−05).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with statistical support and reference to Figure 2d.

claim: CRMs with strong and intermediate conserved binding show stronger sequence conservation than those with no conserved binding.
source: In addition, CRMs with strong and intermediate conserved binding show stronger sequence conservation (Figure 2e)
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with reference to Figure 2e showing PhastCons scores.

claim: Twi, Tin, Mef2 and Bin each occupy their enhancers during D. melanogaster development in three temporal classes: continuously at all stages, and two transient classes occupied only at early or late stages.
source: Twi, Tin, Mef2 and Bin, for example, each occupy their enhancers during D. melanogaster development in three temporal classes (Jakobsen et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2009; Sandmann et al., 2007, 2006): continuously at all stages of development where they are expressed, and two interesting transient classes occupied only at early or late stages of development, despite the TFs being expressed at broader developmental windows.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dynamic patterns of TF occupancy are conserved across large evolutionary distances between D. melanogaster and D. virilis.
source: We now show that these dynamic combinatorial patterns are also maintained across large evolutionary distances, suggesting that these temporal patterns of TF occupancy are functionally important.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on their hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: Almost all motifs specifically enriched in early-bound Twist CRMs are present in both D. melanogaster and D. virilis.
source: Almost all motifs specifically enriched in the early-bound CRMs are present in both species (Figure 3b), suggesting a role, together with Twist, in the regulation of early-bound CRMs.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with reference to Figure 3b showing motif enrichment.

claim: Motifs for Zelda and Dorsal are enriched in early-bound Twist CRMs in both species.
source: This includes motifs for Zelda and Dorsal, two TFs functionally required for Twi binding to a number of early blastoderm enhancers (Jiang and Levine, 1993; Yáñez-Cuna et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Twist-late bound enhancers have more divergence in the additional motifs enriched in each species compared to early-bound enhancers.
source: Interestingly, the Twist-late bound enhancers have more divergence in the additional motifs enriched in each species (Figure 3b), which may reflect the cellular heterogeneity that is being specified during this developmental stage.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with reference to Figure 3b and provides a potential explanation.

claim: Loss of TF binding is associated with a significantly lower density of that TF's motif in D. virilis for all five TFs.
source: In all cases, the loss of TF binding is associated with a significantly lower density of that TF's motif (p-values < 1e-7, binomial test) for each of the five TFs in D. virilis (Figure 4a, compare circles to triangles).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with statistical support and reference to Figure 4a.

claim: When TF binding is lost, the motif densities drop to background averages.
source: Notably, when TF binding is lost, the motif densities drop to background averages (Figure 4a, compare triangles to the bars), indicating that loss of TF occupancy is generally concomitant with loss of functional motifs for that TF (Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: The number of Tin motifs in enhancers with conserved binding decreases as TF binding complexity increases.
source: The number of Tin, and to a lesser extent Mef2 and Bin, motifs (overall motif density) in enhancers with conserved binding (Figure 4a, circles) tends to decrease as TF binding complexity increases (for example 7.96 versus 10.41 Tin motifs/kb (p-value < 5e-7, binomial test) in high-bound versus singleton enhancers, respectively)
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with statistical support and reference to Figure 4a.

claim: There is a significantly lower correlation between TF occupancy predicted from sequence (ΔSTAP) and that observed (ΔChIP) in highly-bound CRMs compared to singleton CRMs for Tin.
source: Repeating the ΔSTAP-ΔChIP analysis for each enhancer category separately (high-bound, low-bound and singletons, Figure 4b) showed a significantly lower correlation between TF occupancy predicted from sequence (ΔSTAP) and that observed (ΔChIP) in highly-bound CRMs compared to singleton CRMs for Tin (Fisher z-transformation, p=0.05, Figure 4b).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with statistical support and reference to Figure 4b.

claim: Tin occupies enhancers in both species despite divergence in its motif when bound with many other TFs (4-5 factors).
source: Our cross-species occupancy data provides the first evidence that this prediction holds true for a collection of elements: in the context of enhancers bound by many TFs (4–5 factors), Tin occupies the enhancer in both species despite divergence in its motif, which is not the case when Tin binds alone (Figure 4a–c).
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on their STAP analysis with reference to Figure 4a-c.

claim: Tin co-associates significantly with Twi, Bap, Mef2, and to a lesser extent with Bin.
source: Indeed, Tin co-associates significantly with three other factors, Twi, Bap and Mef2, and to a lesser extent with Bin.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from their co-association analysis.

claim: Co-associations in TF binding are present in both D. melanogaster and D. virilis.
source: Importantly, these co-associations in binding are present in both species, and therefore maintained across a large evolutionary distance, suggesting that the general properties by which these TFs regulate enhancer activity, and by extension the overall topology of the mesodermal gene regulatory network, is largely conserved.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and its implications.

claim: Four TF pairs show significant binding co-divergence: Tin/Bap, Tin/Twi, Tin/Mef2, and Bap/Bin.
source: Four TF pairs show such a significant binding dependency, which we refer to as co-divergence (Figure 5b, highlighted cells). In concordance with the association analysis (Figure 5a), three of the four cases involve Tin, and include Tin/Bap, Tin/Twi, and Tin/Mef2 (corrected p-values of 6 × 10−11, 0.007, and 0.0006 respectively, Figure 5b,d).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with statistical support and reference to Figure 5b.

claim: Tin and Bap show bidirectional dependency where loss of each TF's occupancy is associated with loss of the other TF's motifs.
source: This analysis also indicates the direction of dependency: Loss of Tin and Bap occupancy is associated with the loss of Bap and Tin motifs, respectively (Figure 5c, p=2.09E−04 and p=8.44E−04, respectively), a bidirectional dependency consistent with cooperative recruitment rather than via a heterodimer motif.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with statistical support and reference to Figure 5c.

claim: Tin and Bap co-bind to 327 CRMs during visceral mesoderm specification.
source: Our results indicate that both TFs have conserved co-binding to hundreds of elements (327 CRMs) during visceral mesoderm specification.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of co-bound CRMs.

claim: Mef2 and Tin exhibit a unidirectional association where the loss of Mef2 occupancy is associated with the loss of Tin motifs but not vice-versa.
source: Mef2 and Tin exhibit a unidirectional association where the loss of Mef2 occupancy is associated with the loss of Tin motifs (p=1.96E−04) but not vice-versa (p=8.05E−01)(Figure 5c).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with statistical support and reference to Figure 5c.

claim: Seven orthologous enhancer pairs with medium to high divergence in TF binding were tested for in-vivo activity in transgenic D. melanogaster embryos.
source: Here we compared the spatio-temporal expression patterns of both D. melanogaster and D. virilis orthologous CRM pairs (Figure 6). For this, we selected pairs with medium to high divergence in TF binding to orthologous CRMs (i.e. a medium to low Jaccard index (J <= 0.5); Supplementary file 10) in addition to having a high SVM specificity (spec. >0.98) of predicted expression for the D. melanogaster CRM. Of the 161 orthologous pairs passing these criteria, we selected seven pairs after manual checking for a good alignment between orthologous loci.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the selection criteria and number of enhancer pairs tested.

claim: Five out of seven CRM pairs (71%) showed conserved tissue activity between D. melanogaster and D. virilis.
source: All 14 CRMs (7 D. melanogaster and their 7 D. virilis orthologs) were assayed in transgenic reporter assays in D. melanogaster (Materials and methods, Supplementary file 10). Five CRM pairs (71%) showed conserved tissue activity between both species (Figure 6a)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and percentage with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: The five orthologous enhancers with conserved tissue activity have extensive divergence in their TF occupancy, with less than 40% of their TF binding conserved (Median Jaccard index = 0.37).
source: Overall, the five orthologous enhancers with conserved tissue activity (output) have extensive divergence in their TF occupancy, with less than 40% of their TF binding conserved (Figure 6a, Median Jaccard index = 0.37).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the conservation level with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: D. mel CRM-3215 is bound by all five TFs in D. melanogaster while in D. virilis it is only bound by Mef2.
source: For example, D. mel CRM-3215 is bound by all five TFs in D. melanogaster while in D. virilis it is only bound by Mef2 (Figure 6b).
evidence: The manuscript states this specific example with reference to Figure 6b showing the binding data.

claim: D. mel CRM-1560 is bound by Tin, Bap and Bin in D. melanogaster, but all significant binding for these factors is lost in D. virilis while the enhancer gained Mef2 binding, yet the visceral muscle activity is conserved.
source: Even more striking is D. mel CRM-1560, which is bound by Tin, Bap and Bin in melanogaster (Figure 6c). All significant binding for these factors is lost in D. virilis (CRM 2469), but the enhancer has gained Mef2 binding – yet the very specific VM activity is conserved (Jaccard index = 0, Figure 6a,c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this specific example with reference to Figure 6c and supplementary figure.

claim: Divergence in TF binding does not necessarily equate to divergence in enhancer activity.
source: These data indicate that divergence in TF binding does not necessarily equate to divergence in enhancer activity, as generally assumed.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on their transgenic reporter assay results.

claim: The strong conservation in orthologous enhancer output despite low conservation in TF binding may reflect stabilizing selection acting to maintain the correct spatio-temporal activity of orthologous developmental enhancers.
source: The strong conservation in orthologous enhancer output, despite a low conservation in TF binding may reflect stabilizing selection acting to maintain the correct spatio-temporal activity of orthologous developmental enhancers.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this interpretation of their findings.

claim: TFs higher up in the mesodermal gene regulatory network (Twi and Tin) generally have more conserved occupancy (~54%) compared to TFs lower down in the network (Bap and Bin; 19% and 25% respectively).
source: The TFs higher up in the network (Twi and Tin) generally have more conserved occupancy (~54%) compared to TFs lower down in the network (Bap and Bin; 19% and 25% respectively) (Figure 1a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with specific percentages and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Twi directly regulates tin expression.
source: Twi directly regulates tin expression (Yin et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yin et al., 1997.

claim: Tin regulates bap expression.
source: Tin regulates bap (Lee and Frasch, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee and Frasch, 2005.

claim: Bap regulates bin expression.
source: Bap in turn regulates bin expression (Zaffran et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zaffran et al., 2001.

claim: The TFs examined in this study have a conserved role in mesoderm specification and muscle development from flies to man.
source: The TFs examined in this study have a conserved role in mesoderm specification and muscle development from flies to man, and form part of an evolutionarily conserved GRN.
evidence: The manuscript states this based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Embryogenesis takes approximately 10 hours longer in D. virilis compared to D. melanogaster.
source: The life cycle from egg lay to adult between D. virilis and D. melanogaster is temporally different, with embryogenesis taking ~10 hr longer in D. virilis compared to D. melanogaster (Markow et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Markow et al., 2009.

claim: The D. virilis non-coding genome is approximately 50% larger than D. melanogaster.
source: potentially reflecting the larger size of the D. virilis non-coding genome (which we estimate is approximately 50% larger)
evidence: The manuscript provides an estimate of the genome size difference.

claim: ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq signal for Mef2 over D. melanogaster CRMs are highly correlated (Pearson correlation R² = 0.75).
source: Although the D. melanogaster data is ChIP-chip and D. virilis ChIP-seq, the TF occupancy patterns from the chromatin immunoprecipitation are highly correlated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing the correlation.

claim: STAP models fit the ChIP data very well, with average Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) = 0.51 over the 28 data sets.
source: The models fit the data very well, with PCC = 0.51 being the average over the 28 data sets (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the correlation value for STAP model performance.

claim: The average PCC for STAP analysis in previous analysis of 45 different ChIP data sets was approximately 0.30.
source: For comparison, the average PCC in our previous analysis of 45 different ChIP data sets (also using 2000 segments) was ~0.30 (Cheng et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2013.

claim: Tin and Bap were suggested to bind as a heterodimer to one enhancer in D. melanogaster.
source: Tin and Bap were suggested to bind as a heterodimer to one enhancer in D. melanogaster (Zaffran and Frasch, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zaffran and Frasch, 2002.

claim: Tin directly regulates bap expression, representing a conserved feed forward loop on 327 developmental enhancers.
source: As Tin directly regulates bap expression, this represents a conserved feed forward loop on these 327 developmental enhancers.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on their co-divergence analysis and known regulatory relationships.
